newsitem.title: UK: Mixed reception for NatWest Markets deal.
newsitem.headline: Mixed reception for NatWest Markets deal.

text.p: Joe Ortiz
National Westminster Bank's takeover of prominent corporate finance boutique J O Hambro Magan to beef up its insignificant corporate finance operation got a mixed reception on Friday.

Some analysts voiced concern over the timing of the deal and NatWest was also attacked for paying large sums to lock in the services of its current and newly acquired corporate financiers while it runs down its branch network.
Run by George Magan, Hambro Magan has been involved in some of the bigest mergers and acquisitions in Britain in recent years.

But some banking analysts said the timing of the deal looked as though Magan had spotted the peak of the market and wanted to cash in although under the terms of the agreement he will be tied by so-called "golden handcuffs" to NatWest for three years.

"This isn't the time to be expanding into corporate finance," said David Poutney, banking analyst at Panmure Gordon. "The equity market could be near its top and six months from now we could have a Labour (Party) government which could curtail merger activity."
Poutney also said that the Hambro Magan business would do nothing to improve NatWest's return on equity.
But other analysts were less scathing. While agreeing that Magan might have smelled the top of the market, John Leonard of Salomon Brothers said the buy made sense for NatWest Markets strategically.
"It makes a lot of sense because NatWest is short in the high-end corporate finance area. They have brought in top names, hopefully they will produce," Leonard said
Analaysts said a lot would depend on George Magan's personal commitment to the alliance.

Newspaper reports on Friday said Magan and his associates have a cut a generous deal with NatWest which involves them staying for three years. Some of NatWest's existing corporate finance staff will also gain.

But on Friday, NatWest Markets took the unusual step of rebutting some of what it called "inaccurate and purely speculative" coverage of the deal which suggested that 120 corporate financiers would recieve two million pounds each.
Based on revenues produced by Hambro Magan, most analysts think the deal could have cost NatWest around 80 million pounds ($126 million).
NatWest defended itself for including an element that was designed to keep the "high quality people" that come with the deal.
Hambro Magan has advised on transactions worth over 18 billion pounds since it was founded in 1988.

In a recent league table of dealmaking activity, Hambro Magan was in 15th place with 1.6 billion pounds of deals done in the year to September. NatWest Markets was a lowly 18th with 247 million pounds of deals.
The list was headed by N M Rothschild with 8.5 billion pounds.
The "golden handcuffs" deal provoked outrage from union leaders of NatWest's relatively lowly paid clerical staff.
"These pay outs are an insult to the 20,000 staff that NatWest Bank have already made redundant in their High Street (retail branch banking) operation," said BIFU general secretary Ed Sweeney.

But NatWest is having to pay through the nose because competition for top names in corporate finance is fierce as firms like ING Barings, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, SBC Warburg and the rest compete, expensively, for the "best" people.

As well as Magan himself, the deal brings his deputy Alton Irby to NatWest and Sir Michael Richardson, formerly head of broker Smith New Court, who includes a passion for fox hunting among his non-finance pastimes.
NatWest said the Hambro Magan buy was an ideal fit with its purchase of Gleacher in the United States last year.
Analysts said further in-fill buys could be made for the investment bank but that the retail bank is still looking to build its capability in life insurance and pensions.
